title: A Computational Modeling Approach to Investigate the Influence of Hyperthermia on the Tumor Microenvironment
protocol: Build the model of a bipolar radiofrequency system using COMSOL Multiphysics.
Launch COMSOL Multiphysics and click on Model Wizard.
Select 3D as Space Dimension.
Select AC/DC Physics module | Electric Fields and Currents | Electric Currents.
Select Heat Transfer module | Heat Transfer in Solids.
Select Mathematics module | PDE interfaces | Coefficient Form PDE.
Select Study | Time-dependent.
Click on Done.
Once the Comsol working space appears, select Multiphysics | Electromagnetic Heating.
Define two cones with dimensions listed in Table 2.
Position the cones at the distance indicated in Table 2 (spaced dinter-el apart).
Duplicate the two previous cones to model the insulation of the needles.
Modify the size of the cone according to the dimensions reported in Table 2.
Select a cylinder to model the bulk of muscle placed at z = -9 mm (x = 0, y = 0).
Select a cylinder to model the thin layer of skin placed at z = 4 mm (x = 0, y = 0).
Select a sphere to model the subcutaneous tumor placed at z = -0.5 mm (x = 0, y = 0).
From the Geometry ribbon, select Virtual operations | Form Composite Domains.
Select all domains related to the electrically conductive part of the needles to create a composite geometry.
Repeat the procedure to create composite domains for the needle insulation geometries.
Define properties of the biological tissue models.
Right-click on Component node and select Definitions.
Under Functions, select Analytic.
Specify the name of the Function (e.g., k_muscle or sigma_muscle).
Type the mathematical expression consistent with Eq. 2).
Specify temperature (T) as argument.
Specify units of the function: S/m in the case of electrical conductivity.
From Materials, select More Materials | Porous Material.
Right-click on Porous Material to select Fluid and Solid components.
Select Fluid node and under Fluid properties, select Blood (defined in the previous steps).
Select Solid node and under Solid properties, select Tumor (defined in the previous steps).
In the Solid node, specify the volume fraction defined as θS (Table 1).
Enable manual selection and select the geometric entity corresponding to the specified material.
Under Mesh node, select Size and select a predefined Finer mesh.
Add Free Tetrahedral feature under Mesh node.
Select geometries of interest and customize maximum element size to 0.25 mm.
Customize minimum element size ensuring smallest component is discretized by at least four meshing elements.
Right-click on the Electric Currents node.
For Terminal, manually select the proximal end (on the top) of one of the two needles.
Under Terminal, select Power and specify value according to desired energy protocol.
Select 0.5 W for mild hyperthermia based on preliminary ex vivo experiments.
Manually select the proximal surface of the second needle under Ground node.
Apply electrical insulation to the remaining external surface of the model.
Select Heat Transfer in Solids node and specify 33 °C as the initial value of the temperature.
Right-click on Heat Transfer in Solids, add the Heat source domain, and select the geometry where the heat sink effect should be considered.
Type the expression for the heat sink in General Source | User defined.
For thermal boundary conditions, right-click on Heat Transfer, add Heat Flux as a boundary condition, and specify external surfaces.
Select Convective heat flux as the flux type.
Specify the heat transfer coefficient h = 15 W/(m2 ·K).
Use T = 20 °C to model the ambient temperature in the laboratory environment.
Select Coefficient Form PDE node and specify Pressure as the dependent variable.
Specify the time unit as seconds (s).
Set the start time to 0 s.
Set the step interval to 5 s.
Set the stop time to 900 s.
Set the frequency to 500e3 Hz.
Select Compute to run the simulations.
Right-click and select a cut plane, such as the zx-plane at y = 0, to define the plane for visualizing 2D distributions.
Right-click and select a cut point in the 3D volume to display parameter variation over time.
From Results on the top ribbon, select 2D plot group to visualize two-dimensional distribution of a variable (e.g., temperature) on one of the planes identified earlier.
Select 1D plot group to visualize 1D results (e.g., pressure across time) at the point or multiple points identified in previous steps.
